questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A large tank contains water at a uniform temperature to a depth of 20 m. The tank is open to the atmosphere and atmospheric pressure is equivalent to that of 10 m of water. An air bubble is released from the bottom of the tank and rises to the surface. The air bubbles behave like an ideal gas.

Assuming surface tension effects to be negligible, what happens to the volume of the air bubble?
questions.stemText: A large tank contains water at a uniform temperature to a depth of 20 m. The tank is open to the atmosphere and atmospheric pressure is equivalent to that of 10 m of water. An air bubble is released from the bottom of the tank and rises to the surface. The air bubbles behave like an ideal gas. Assuming surface tension effects to be negligible, what happens to the volume of the air bubble? A Doubles when it reaches the surface B Triples when it reaches the surface C Halves when it reaches the surface D Remains constant

options.label: A
options.text: Doubles when it reaches the surface

options.label: B
options.text: Triples when it reaches the surface

options.label: C
options.text: Halves when it reaches the surface

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must include atmospheric pressure at both depths and use the inverse pressure–volume relation.
questions.misconception: Ignoring atmospheric pressure at the bottom

explanation.body: With the amount of gas and temperature constant, $pV=nRT$ gives $p_1V_1=p_2V_2$. The pressures at the bottom and surface are equivalent to $30\ \mathrm m$ and $10\ \mathrm m$ of water, respectively. Thus $30V_1=10V_2$ and $V_2=3V_1$.

perOption.A: Uses the water pressure alone at the bottom and omits the atmospheric contribution there.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the pressure–volume relation and predicts compression as the bubble rises.
perOption.D: Assumes constant temperature implies constant volume even though pressure decreases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Five gas molecules have the following velocities:

velocity / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 250 | 300 | 400 | 100 | 500

What is the root mean square speed?

A $150\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $270\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $750\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 14: Five gas molecules have the following velocities: velocity / m s−1 250 300 400 100 500 What is the root mean square speed?

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The speeds can be substituted directly into the definition of root mean square speed.
questions.misconception: Taking the average outside the square root

explanation.body: Square the five speeds and take their mean. The root mean square speed is $\sqrt{\frac{250^2+300^2+400^2+100^2+500^2}{5}}=340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Divides by five after taking the square root.
perOption.B: Underestimates the root mean square, which must be at least as large as the arithmetic mean of $310\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Takes the square root of the sum of squares without dividing by five first.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An ideal gas is held in a constant volume container fitted with a valve through which gas can escape.

Starting at 150 K, the temperature of the gas is raised by 900 K while its pressure in the container is raised from P to 2P. This results in a fraction of the original number of gas molecules escaping through the valve.

What is the pressure in the container after the gas is cooled back to its starting temperature?
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is held in a constant volume container fitted with a valve through which gas can escape. Starting at 150 K, the temperature of the gas is raised by 900 K while its pressure in the container is raised from P to 2P. This results in a fraction of the original number of gas molecules escaping through the valve. What is the pressure in the container after the gas is cooled back to its starting temperature? A 0.29 P B 0.33 P C 0.50 P D P

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must choose the post-leak state and use the absolute hot temperature.
questions.misconception: Treating the temperature increase as the final temperature.

explanation.body: After heating and leakage, the gas is at $1050\ \mathrm{K}$ and pressure $2P$. During cooling, assume no further gas escapes, so $p/T$ is constant at fixed volume. The final pressure is $2P(150/1050)=0.29P$.

perOption.A: Correct. It scales the post-leak pressure by $150/1050$.
perOption.B: Uses the temperature rise of $900\ \mathrm{K}$ as the hot temperature.
perOption.C: Assumes a pressure decrease by a factor of two even though the absolute temperature falls by a factor of seven.
perOption.D: Assumes the original pressure returns when the original temperature returns, overlooking the loss of gas.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A fixed amount of an ideal gas has pressure $p$ and volume $V$.

The graph shows the variation of $\frac{1}{p}$ with $V$ at a constant temperature.

[Graph of $1/p$ vertically against $V$ horizontally, with a straight line from the origin to the top-right corner of a square grid.]

The amount of gas and the thermodynamic temperature are then both decreased by half.

Which line shows the variation of $\frac{1}{p}$ with $V$?

[The second graph has the same axes and shows the original line dashed. Four solid lines pass through the origin. A and B reach the top of the grid at one quarter and one half of its width, respectively. C and D reach the right edge at one half and one quarter of its height, respectively.]

stemImage.alt: Question 12: A fixed amount of an ideal gas has pressure p and volume V. The graph shows the variation of 1 with V at a constant temperature. p The amount of gas and the the

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Rearranging the gas law exposes how the two changes combine in the graph gradient.
questions.misconception: Treating gradient as proportional to the amount of gas and temperature.

explanation.body: The ideal gas equation $pV=nRT$ gives $1/p=V/(nRT)$. Halving both $n$ and $T$ reduces $nRT$ to one quarter of its original value, so the gradient becomes four times as large. This is line A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Doubles the gradient by accounting for only one of the two changes.
perOption.C: Halves the gradient as if it were directly proportional to only one of the changed quantities.
perOption.D: Quarters the gradient as if it were directly proportional to the product of amount and temperature.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which is not an assumption of the kinetic theory of gas?
questions.stemText: Which is not an assumption of the kinetic theory of gas? A The motion of the molecules is random. B The molecules move at various speeds. C The volume of the molecules is comparable with the volume of the container. D All collisions of molecules with each other and with the container walls are perfectly elastic.

options.label: A
options.text: The motion of the molecules is random.

options.label: B
options.text: The molecules move at various speeds.

options.label: C
options.text: The volume of the molecules is comparable with the volume of the container.

options.label: D
options.text: All collisions of molecules with each other and with the container walls are perfectly elastic.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The question asks for direct recall of the ideal-gas particle volume assumption.
questions.misconception: Treating molecular volume as comparable to container volume.

explanation.body: The kinetic theory assumes that the molecules together occupy a negligible fraction of the container's volume. Option C instead treats the volumes as comparable.

perOption.A: Random molecular motion is part of the model.
perOption.B: The model allows a distribution of molecular speeds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Perfectly elastic collisions are part of the model.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An isolated container is divided into two sections of equal volumes by a partition. The ideal gas in each section has the same pressure $P$.

What is the final pressure after the partition is removed?

A $\tfrac12P$
B $P$
C $\tfrac32P$
D $2P$

stemImage.alt: Question 9: An isolated container is divided into two sections of equal volumes by a partition. The ideal gas in each section has the same pressure P. What is the final pre

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must account for the gas initially present in both halves when the volume available to each portion doubles.
questions.misconception: Treating one compartment as a vacuum.

explanation.body: The key treats the two portions as initially at the same temperature, as they would be if they contained equal amounts of gas at the given pressure and volume. With the portions initially at the same temperature, removing the partition leaves the temperature and pressure unchanged, so the final pressure is $P$.

perOption.A: Accounts for expansion into twice the volume but counts only the gas from one half.
perOption.B: Correct. Both halves contribute to the final pressure.
perOption.C: Counts one half’s original pressure in full and halves only the other half’s contribution.
perOption.D: Adds the two original pressures without allowing each portion to spread through twice its original volume.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A fixed volume container contains a mixture of two monatomic gases X and Y at the same temperature. The mass of the molecules of X is twice that of molecules of Y.

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{root mean square speed of molecules of X}}{\text{root mean square speed of molecules of Y}}$?

A 0.50
B 0.71
C 1.4
D 2.0

stemImage.alt: Question 10: A fixed volume container contains a mixture of two monatomic gases X and Y at the same temperature. The mass of the molecules of X is twice that of molecules of

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish the inverse-mass scaling of mean-square speed from the scaling of RMS speed.
questions.misconception: Treating RMS speed as inversely proportional to molecular mass.

explanation.body: At the same temperature, both gases have the same mean molecular kinetic energy $\tfrac12m\langle c^2\rangle$. Thus $\langle c^2\rangle\propto1/m$, and $c_{\mathrm{rms},X}/c_{\mathrm{rms},Y}=\sqrt{m_Y/m_X}=\sqrt{1/2}=0.71$.

perOption.A: Uses the inverse mass ratio directly without taking its square root.
perOption.B: Correct. RMS speed scales as the inverse square root of mass.
perOption.C: Reverses the mass ratio under the square root.
perOption.D: Uses the direct mass ratio and omits the square root.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: In deriving the equation $p = \frac{1}{3}\rho\langle c^2\rangle$ in the simple kinetic theory of gases, which statement is not taken as a valid assumption? A Attractive forces between the molecules are negligible. B The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas. C The duration of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions. D The molecules suffer negligible change of momentum on collision with the walls of the container.

stemImage.alt: Question 17: 1 =  2 p c In deriving the equation in the simple kinetic theory of gases, which 3 statement is not taken as a valid assumption?

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall of kinetic theory assumptions with one invalid statement to spot.
questions.misconception: Confusing elastic collisions (no KE change) with no momentum change

explanation.body:
When a molecule collides elastically with a wall, its velocity reverses, so the magnitude of its change in momentum is twice its momentum before the collision. This change is not negligible; it is what produces the pressure.

So D is not a valid assumption.

perOption.A: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.B: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.C: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.D: Correct. The momentum change $2mu$ per collision is what causes the pressure.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A cylinder, closed by a moveable piston, contains an ideal gas at 50 °C and atmospheric pressure $1.0\times10^{5}$ Pa. The piston is moved out until the volume of the gas doubles and the temperature falls to 25 °C. What is the new pressure of the gas in the cylinder? A $1.6\times10^{4}$ Pa B $2.5\times10^{4}$ Pa C $4.6\times10^{4}$ Pa D $1.9\times10^{5}$ Pa

stemImage.alt: Question 18: A cylinder, closed by a moveable piston, contains an ideal gas at 50 C and atmospheric pressure 1.0  105 Pa. The piston is moved out until the volume of the g

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct ideal-gas ratio calculation with a Celsius-to-kelvin conversion.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperatures instead of kelvin

explanation.body:
Since $pV = nRT$, $p \propto \dfrac{T}{V}$ ($n$ and $R$ constant), so $\dfrac{p'}{p} = \left(\dfrac{T'}{T}\right)\left(\dfrac{V}{V'}\right)$.

$p' = \left(\dfrac{273.15+25}{273.15+50}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)(1.0\times10^{5}) = 4.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

perOption.A: Does not follow from $p \propto T/V$; mishandles the temperature or volume ratio.
perOption.B: Uses Celsius temperatures instead of kelvin.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Multiplies by the volume ratio instead of dividing (treats $p \propto V$).

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An ideal gas is contained in two spherical containers X and Y of volume $2V$ and $V$ respectively, connected by a hollow tube of negligible volume. The containers X and Y are maintained at temperatures $2T$ and $T$ respectively. The setup is shown in the diagram below.

[The larger sphere X is labelled $2V$ and $2T$. A horizontal tube joins it to the smaller sphere Y, labelled $V$ and $T$.]

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{number of moles of gas in container X}}{\text{number of moles of gas in container Y}}$?

A 0.25
B 1
C 2
D 4

stemImage.alt: Question 12: An ideal gas is contained in two spherical containers X and Y of volume 2V and V respectively, connected by a hollow tube of negligible volume. The containers X

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer equal pressures and account for simultaneous changes in volume and temperature.
questions.misconception: Assuming that equal pressure also requires equal temperature.

explanation.body: For container X, $p_X=n_X R(2T)/(2V)=n_XRT/V$. For container Y, $p_Y=n_YRT/V$. The tube connects the gases, so $p_X=p_Y$ and hence $n_X/n_Y=1$.

perOption.A: Inverts the volume ratio while also halving the result for X’s higher temperature.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the volume ratio alone and ignores the temperature difference.
perOption.D: Treats the amount of gas as directly proportional to temperature and volume at equal pressure.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The density of an ideal gas is $1.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ at a pressure of $1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

What is the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) speed of the molecules of the gas?

A $350\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $500\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $3700\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $2.50\times10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 12: The density of an ideal gas is 1.2 kg m−3 at a pressure of 1.0 × 105 Pa. What is the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) speed of the molecules of the gas?

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must replace mass per volume with density and take the square root after rearranging.
questions.misconception: Confusing mean square speed with root-mean-square speed

explanation.body: From kinetic theory, $P=\frac13(Nm/V)\langle c^2\rangle=\frac13\rho\langle c^2\rangle$. Substitution gives $1.0\times10^5=\frac13(1.2)\langle c^2\rangle$. Therefore $\sqrt{\langle c^2\rangle}=500\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Using $3/2$ in place of the factor 3 when solving for mean square speed gives about this value.
perOption.B: Correct. This is the square root of $3P/ho$.
perOption.C: A speed of 3700 m/s would imply a pressure far above the one given.
perOption.D: Reports the mean square speed and omits the square root.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An ideal gas has thermodynamic temperature $T$, and its molecules have root-mean-square speed $c_{rms}$. If the gas is heated to temperature $2T$, what is the new r.m.s. speed? A $\sqrt{2}c_{rms}$ B $2c_{rms}$ C $2\sqrt{2}c_{rms}$ D $4c_{rms}$

stemImage.alt: Question 14: An ideal gas has thermodynamic temperature T, and its molecules has root-mean-square c speed . If the gas is heated to temperature 2T, what is the new root-mean

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One-step use of $c_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$.
questions.misconception: Assuming r.m.s. speed is proportional to temperature

explanation.body: The mean translational kinetic energy satisfies $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, so $c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\propto T$. Hence $T/(2T)=c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}^2$, which gives $c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}=\sqrt{2}\,c_{\mathrm{rms}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the rms speed itself as directly proportional to temperature.
perOption.C: Applies an extra factor of two after taking the square root of the temperature ratio.
perOption.D: Squares the temperature ratio instead of taking its square root.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is contained in two spherical containers X and Y of volume $2V$ and $V$ respectively, connected by a hollow tube of negligible volume. X and Y are maintained at temperatures $2T$ and $T$ respectively. [Diagram: large sphere X labelled $2V, 2T$ joined by a thin tube to small sphere Y labelled $V, T$.] Determine the ratio (number of moles of gas in X)/(number of moles of gas in Y). A 0.25 B 1.00 C 2.00 D 4.00

stemImage.alt: Question 15: An ideal gas is contained in two spherical containers X and Y of volume 2V and V respectively, connected by a hollow tube of negligible volume. The containers X

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that connected containers share a common pressure, then comparing V/T.
questions.misconception: Ignoring that the pressure is equal in connected containers, or mishandling the V/T ratio

explanation.body: The connected containers have the same pressure $p$ at equilibrium. Using $n=pV/(RT)$ gives $n_X=p(2V)/[R(2T)]=pV/(RT)$ and $n_Y=pV/(RT)$. The school's working therefore gives $n_X/n_Y=1.00$, even though its answer label is A.

perOption.A: Inverts the volume ratio while keeping the temperature ratio in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct. The volume and temperature factors cancel.
perOption.C: Accounts for the doubled volume but ignores the doubled temperature.
perOption.D: Treats the amount of gas as directly proportional to temperature at fixed pressure and volume.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Helium molecules have a r.m.s. speed of 1800 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at 20 °C.

The mass of a neon molecule is five times the mass of a helium molecule.

What is the r.m.s. speed of molecules of neon at the same temperature?
questions.stemText: Helium molecules have a r.m.s. speed of 1800 m s–1 at 20 °C. The mass of a neon molecule is five times the mass of a helium molecule. What is the r.m.s. speed of molecules of neon at the same temperature? A 360 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 800 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 4000 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 9000 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Same temperature means same mean KE, giving $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the square root in $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$

explanation.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12 m c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32 kT$, so at the same temperature $m\propto1/c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$. For neon, $m/(5m)=c_{\mathrm{Ne}}^2/1800^2$, giving $c_{\mathrm{Ne}}=804.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx800\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides the speed by five instead of dividing by the square root of five.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes r.m.s. speed increase with the square root of mass.
perOption.D: Makes r.m.s. speed directly proportional to mass.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A rigid cylinder contains 19 kg of compressed air at 9.5 times atmospheric pressure and 7 °C.

It is heated to 27 °C. A safety valve releases air whenever the pressure exceeds 10 times atmospheric pressure.

Assuming the air behaves as an ideal gas, what mass of air escapes?
questions.stemText: A rigid cylinder contains 19 kg of compressed air at 9.5 times atmospheric pressure and 7 °C. It is heated to 27 °C. A safety valve releases air whenever the pressure exceeds 10 times atmospheric pressure. Assuming the air behaves as an ideal gas, what mass of air escapes? A 0.18 kg B 0.33 kg C 0.68 kg D 13.8 kg

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Ideal gas law at constant volume with changing mass and kelvin conversion.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius instead of kelvin temperatures

explanation.body: From $pV=nRT$, at fixed cylinder volume $p\propto nT$. Thus $9.5/10=n_1(273.15+7)/[n_2(273.15+27)]$, giving $n_2=0.98249n_1$. Mass is proportional to amount of gas, so $m_2=0.98249(19)=18.667\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $19-18.667\approx0.33\ \mathrm{kg}$ escapes.

perOption.A: Underestimates the loss by leaving too much gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the loss by leaving too little gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.D: Uses a temperature ratio based on Celsius readings instead of absolute temperatures.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A balloon contains 2.0 moles of helium gas at a temperature of 27 ⁰C. The molar mass of helium is 4.0 g $\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$.

What is the average translational kinetic energy of a helium atom in the balloon?
questions.stemText: A balloon contains 2.0 moles of helium gas at a temperature of 27 ⁰C. The molar mass of helium is 4.0 g mol-1. What is the average translational kinetic energy of a helium atom in the balloon? A 5.6  $10^{-22}$ J B 6.2  $10^{-21}$ J C 30 J D 7500 J

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf
grail:14564 MI 2024 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Single substitution into the mean KE formula after converting to kelvin; the moles and molar mass are red herrings.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperature or computing the total kinetic energy of the gas instead of per atom

explanation.body: The average translational kinetic energy of one helium atom is $\frac32 kT$, with $T$ in kelvin. Substituting gives $\frac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(27+273.15)=6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Substitutes $27$ directly instead of converting the temperature to kelvin.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The calculation must use the Boltzmann constant to obtain the energy per atom.
perOption.D: Uses the energy of the full $2.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ of helium.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two flasks P and Q contain an ideal gas and are connected with a tube of negligible volume compared to that of the flasks. The volume of P is triple the volume of Q. [Diagram: large flask P connected by a thin tube to a smaller flask Q] P is held at a temperature of 200 K and Q is held at a temperature of 600 K. What is the $\dfrac{\text{mass of gas in P}}{\text{mass of gas in Q}}$? A $\frac{1}{9}$ B $\frac{1}{3}$ C 3 D 9

stemImage.alt: Question 12: Two flasks P and Q contain an ideal gas and are connected with a tube of negligible volume compared to that of the flasks. The volume of P is triple the volume

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising equal pressure in connected flasks and combining the volume and temperature ratios.
questions.misconception: Ignoring that the connected flasks share the same pressure, or inverting the temperature dependence

explanation.body: At steady state the pressures in the two flasks are equal. The ideal gas law gives $\frac{n_PRT_P}{V_P}=\frac{n_QRT_Q}{V_Q}$. Since both flasks contain the same gas, $\frac{M_P}{M_Q}=\frac{n_P}{n_Q}=\frac{T_Q}{T_P}\frac{V_P}{V_Q}=3\times3=9$.

perOption.A: Reverses the requested mass ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the inverse volume ratio and misses the temperature difference.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two factors of three.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two vessels A and B of volume $V$ and $8V$ respectively are connected by a tube of negligible volume and contain an ideal gas at an initial temperature of $10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Vessel A initially contains $n$ moles of the ideal gas. Its temperature is then raised to $80\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ while the temperature of B is maintained at $10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. How many moles of gas will be transferred between the vessels when steady state is reached? A $0.18n$ B $0.21n$ C $0.82n$ D $0.86n$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: Two vessels A and B of volume V and 8V respectively are connected by a tube of negligible volume and contain an ideal gas at an initial temperature of 10 C. Ve

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf
grail:16195 2019 RI Prelims Paper 1 QP
grail:19918 TJC 2025 H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Needs conservation of total moles with equal final pressures and kelvin temperatures.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperatures or assuming moles stay proportional to volume

explanation.body: Initially, the ideal gas law gives a total of $9pV/(283R)$ moles at common pressure $p$. At steady state, conservation of moles gives $p'V/(353R)+8p'V/(283R)=9pV/(283R)$, so $p'=1.022530p$. The fraction remaining in A is $1.022530(283/353)=0.819762$, so about $0.18n$ moles leave A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the transfer by leaving less gas in A than the final common pressure requires.
perOption.C: Reports the amount remaining in A as the amount transferred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the transfer by leaving only $0.14n$ in A.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which is not an assumption of the kinetic theory of gases?
questions.stemText: Which is not an assumption of the kinetic theory of gases? A The molecules move at the same speeds. B The motion of the molecules is random. C The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas. D There are negligible forces of attraction or repulsion between molecules except during collisions.

options.label: A
options.text: The molecules move at the same speeds.

options.label: B
options.text: The motion of the molecules is random.

options.label: C
options.text: The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.

options.label: D
options.text: There are negligible forces of attraction or repulsion between molecules except during collisions.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the kinetic theory assumptions.
questions.misconception: Believing all gas molecules have the same speed

explanation.body: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas, molecules move randomly with a range of speeds. The temperature fixes their mean translational kinetic energy, so equal molecular speeds are unnecessary.

perOption.A: Correct. Molecules can have different speeds.
perOption.B: Random molecular motion is an assumption of the model.
perOption.C: The model treats the molecules’ own volume as negligible compared with the gas volume.
perOption.D: The model neglects intermolecular forces between collisions.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
P and Q are two different ideal gases contained in two separate identical vessels and the masses of their molecules are $M_P$ and $M_Q$ respectively.

The ratio of their thermodynamic temperatures, $T_P$ and $T_Q$, and that of the root-mean-square speeds of their molecules, $c_P$ and $c_Q$, are

$\dfrac{T_P}{T_Q} = 2$ and $\dfrac{c_P}{c_Q} = 3$.

What is the value of $\dfrac{M_P}{M_Q}$?

A $\dfrac{1}{6}$   B $\dfrac{2}{9}$   C $\dfrac{2}{3}$   D $\dfrac{9}{2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: P and Q are two different ideal gases contained in two separate identical vessels and the masses of their molecules are MP and MQ respectively. The ratio of the

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A direct ratio calculation from the mean kinetic energy formula.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square the r.m.s. speed ratio

explanation.body:
The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac{1}{2}M\langle c^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so

$\dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}M_P c_P^2}{\tfrac{1}{2}M_Q c_Q^2} = \dfrac{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_P}{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_Q}$

$\dfrac{M_P}{M_Q} = \dfrac{T_P}{T_Q} \times \dfrac{c_Q^2}{c_P^2} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3^2} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

perOption.A: Inverts the temperature ratio and forgets to square the speed ratio: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{3}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $M \propto T/c^2$.
perOption.C: Forgets to square the r.m.s. speed ratio.
perOption.D: Inverts the whole ratio, giving $M_Q/M_P$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A closed container is filled with ideal gas initially at a temperature of 27 $^{\mathrm{o}}$C and atmospheric pressure. It was then placed into a hot water bath maintained at 80 $^{\mathrm{o}}$C where the container achieved thermal equilibrium with the hot water bath as shown below.

When the container is opened while immersed in the hot water bath, some of the gas escapes the container.

What is the percentage of the original amount of ideal gas remaining in the container at equilibrium state?
questions.stemText: A closed container is filled with ideal gas initially at a temperature of 27 oC and atmospheric pressure. It was then placed into a hot water bath maintained at 80 oC where the container achieved thermal equilibrium with the hot water bath as shown below. 80 oC hot water bath When the container is opened while immersed in the hot water bath, some of the gas escapes the container. What is the percentage of the original amount of ideal gas remaining in the container at equilibrium state? A 15% B 34% C 66% D 85%

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing gas states at equal pressure and converting both temperatures to kelvin.
questions.misconception: Reporting the fraction that escapes

explanation.body: Once released, the gas expands until it reaches atmospheric pressure, the same as its initial pressure. At that pressure the original amount of gas would occupy $V'$ at $80^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with $V/(273+27)=V'/(273+80)$ and hence $V'=(353/300)V$. The container still has volume $V$, so it retains $V/V'=300/353\approx85\%$ of the original gas.

perOption.A: Gives the percentage that escapes.
perOption.B: Uses the Celsius temperatures directly and treats $27/80$ as the remaining fraction.
perOption.C: Uses the complement of the incorrect Celsius ratio.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An ideal gas is held in a constant volume container fitted with a valve through which gas can escape.

Starting at 250 K, the temperature of the gas is raised by 1000 K while its pressure in the container is allowed to double.

What fraction of the original number of gas molecules escape through the valve?
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is held in a constant volume container fitted with a valve through which gas can escape. Starting at 250 K, the temperature of the gas is raised by 1000 K while its pressure in the container is allowed to double. What fraction of the original number of gas molecules escape through the valve? A 0.4 B 0.5 C 0.6 D 0.9

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires using the final absolute temperature and distinguishing the escaped fraction from the remaining fraction.
questions.misconception: Reporting the fraction remaining

explanation.body: Using $pV=NkT$, the initial state gives $pV=Nk(250)$ and the final state gives $2pV=N'k(1250)$. The fraction that escapes is $(N-N')/N=\left(\frac{pV}{250k}-\frac{2pV}{1250k}\right)\frac{250k}{pV}=0.6$.

perOption.A: Gives the fraction of molecules remaining in the container.
perOption.B: Results from using $1000\ \mathrm{K}$ as the final temperature instead of the temperature rise.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Would leave only one tenth of the molecules, which at five times the temperature would halve the original pressure.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: In the derivation of the relationship between the pressure, the number density of molecules and the mean square speed of the molecules of an ideal gas, which of the following is not an essential assumption?
questions.stemText: In the derivation of the relationship between the pressure, the number density of molecules and the mean square speed of the molecules of an ideal gas, which of the following is not an essential assumption? A that the number of molecules per unit volume is large B that all collisions are elastic C that there are no intermolecular forces of attraction D that the average kinetic energy of a molecule is proportional to the temperature of the gas

options.label: A
options.text: that the number of molecules per unit volume is large

options.label: C
options.text: that there are no intermolecular forces of attraction

options.label: D
options.text: that the average kinetic energy of a molecule is proportional to the temperature of the gas

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing the mechanical assumptions behind gas pressure from a later result about temperature.
questions.misconception: Treating the temperature relation as an input to the pressure derivation

explanation.body: Gas pressure comes from momentum transferred to the walls in elastic collisions. Averaging over many freely moving molecules, with isotropic velocities, gives $p=\tfrac13(N/V)m\langle c^2\rangle$. This derivation uses molecular speeds without a temperature relation. Comparing it with $pV=NkT$ then gives the proportionality between mean kinetic energy and temperature.

perOption.A: A large molecular population in a representative volume supports the statistical average used to describe steady pressure.
perOption.B: Elastic wall collisions give the momentum change used to calculate pressure.
perOption.C: Neglecting intermolecular attraction allows the model to treat molecules as moving freely between collisions.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: An ideal gas is held in a container of volume V at pressure P. The root-mean-squared (rms) speed of a gas molecule under these conditions is u. If the volume and pressure are now changed to 2V and 2P, the rms speed of a molecule will be
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is held in a container of volume V at pressure P. The root-mean-squared (rms) speed of a gas molecule under these conditions is u. If the volume and pressure are now changed to 2V and 2P, the rms speed of a molecule will be A u B 2 u C 2u D 4u

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must combine the ideal-gas law with the square-root dependence of rms speed on temperature.
questions.misconception: Rms speed is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

explanation.body: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, $pV\propto T$, so $T_f/T_i=(p_fV_f)/(p_iV_i)=2\times2=4$. Since $\frac12mv_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac32kT$, the squared speed ratio is also 4. Hence $v_f=2v_i=2u$.

perOption.A: Assumes the temperature stays constant even though $pV$ quadruples.
perOption.B: Counts only one of the two factors of two in $pV$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Scales speed directly with temperature instead of scaling its square.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A sealed tank of gas contains a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. The gas in the tank is at room temperature.

What is the same for the particles of nitrogen and oxygen in the tank?
questions.stemText: A sealed tank of gas contains a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. The gas in the tank is at room temperature. What is the same for the particles of nitrogen and oxygen in the tank? A internal energy B internal energy mean square speed C mean kinetic energy D mean kinetic energy root mean square speed

options.label: D
options.text: mean kinetic energy root mean square speed

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish the temperature dependence of kinetic energy from the mass dependence of speed.
questions.misconception: Gas molecules at the same temperature have the same rms speed.

explanation.body: Both gases have the same temperature, so their molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, $\frac32 kT$. Since this energy is also $\frac12m\langle v^2\rangle$, the lighter nitrogen molecules have a greater mean square speed and rms speed.

perOption.A: Internal energy is a system quantity and can depend on the amount of each gas.
perOption.B: The lighter nitrogen molecules have greater mean square speed at the same temperature.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Taking the square root of the mean square speed preserves the difference between the gases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An ideal gas is placed in a sealed rigid container and heated uniformly.

Which of the following remains constant?
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is placed in a sealed rigid container and heated uniformly. Which of the following remains constant? A average speed of the gas molecules B average distance between the gas molecules C average force acting on the gas molecules by the cylinder wall D average number of molecules hitting the cylinder wall per second

options.label: A
options.text: average speed of the gas molecules

options.label: B
options.text: average distance between the gas molecules

options.label: C
options.text: average force acting on the gas molecules by the cylinder wall

options.label: D
options.text: average number of molecules hitting the cylinder wall per second

appearances.originalFile: grail:15121 TMJC_2024_H2 Physics P1_QP_AS

questions.difficultyReason: Straightforward kinetic-theory reasoning about a constant-volume heating.

explanation.body:
Since the container is sealed and rigid, the volume and the number of molecules stay constant. Hence the average distance between the gas molecules does not change.

Heating raises the temperature, so the molecules move faster and hit the walls harder and more often.

perOption.A: Heating raises the temperature, so the mean kinetic energy and hence the average speed increase.
perOption.B: Correct. Fixed volume and fixed number of molecules means fixed average separation.
perOption.C: Faster molecules undergo larger momentum changes at the wall, so the average force increases (the pressure rises).
perOption.D: Faster molecules reach the walls more often, so the collision rate increases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The root-mean-square speed of molecules of an ideal gas which is at an initial temperature of 350 K, is increased by 20%. What is the new temperature of the ideal gas?
questions.stemText: The root-mean-square speed of molecules of an ideal gas which is at an initial temperature of 350 K, is increased by 20%. What is the new temperature of the ideal gas? A 370 K B 400 K C 420 K D 500 K

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Single proportionality step; the common trap is forgetting to square.
questions.misconception: Assuming temperature is proportional to r.m.s. speed rather than its square

explanation.body:
Mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so $(c_{rms})^2 \propto T$.

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{(1.2\,c_{rms})^2}{c_{rms}^2} = 1.44$

$T_2 = 1.44 \times 350 = 504 \approx 500\ \mathrm{K}$

perOption.A: Treats a 20% increase as adding 20 K to the temperature.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $T \propto c_{rms}^2$; the temperature must rise by a factor of 1.44.
perOption.C: Assumes $T \propto c_{rms}$, giving $1.2 \times 350 = 420\ \mathrm{K}$.
perOption.D: Correct. $T \propto c_{rms}^2$, so $T_2 = 1.2^2 \times 350 \approx 500\ \mathrm{K}$.

A $5\ \mathrm{kg}$
B $14\ \mathrm{kg}$
C $16\ \mathrm{kg}$
D $45\ \mathrm{kg}$

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires identifying the fixed pressure and volume and forming a ratio using absolute temperatures.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperatures in the ideal-gas equation

explanation.body: From $pV=nRT$, the fixed cylinder volume and limiting pressure give $n_1RT_1=n_2RT_2$. With molar mass $M_{\mathrm r}$, this is $\frac{m_1}{M_{\mathrm r}}RT_1=\frac{m_2}{M_{\mathrm r}}RT_2$. Thus $m_2=\frac{273.15+10}{273.15+30}(15)=14.0\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Uses inverse proportionality with temperatures in degrees Celsius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes the mass directly proportional to absolute temperature.
perOption.D: Makes the mass directly proportional to the Celsius temperature.

What is the approximate number of atoms in a cubic metre of an ideal monatomic gas at the temperature of 27 °C and a pressure of $1 \times 10^{5}$ Pa?

A $1 \times 10^{22}$
B $6 \times 10^{23}$
C $2 \times 10^{25}$
D $3 \times 10^{26}$

stemImage.alt: Question 9: What is the approximate number of atoms in a cubic metre of an ideal monatomic gas at the temperature of 27 C and a pressure of 1 x 105 Pa?

questions.misconception: Using temperature in °C in the ideal gas equation

perOption.A: Far too small; does not follow from $N = pV/kT$.
perOption.B: This is the Avogadro constant (one mole), but 1 m³ of gas at these conditions holds about 40 mol.
perOption.C: Correct. $N = pV/kT = 2.4 \times 10^{25}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A fixed mass of monatomic ideal gas at a volume V at temperature T and pressure P has a root mean square speed c. After absorbing heat, its final volume is V and final pressure is 2P. What is the new root mean square speed of the ideal gas?
questions.stemText: A fixed mass of monatomic ideal gas at a volume V at temperature T and pressure P has a root mean square speed c. After absorbing heat, its final volume is V and final pressure is 2P. What is the new root mean square speed of the ideal gas? A 0.5 c B 0.71 c C 1.4 c D 2.0 c

appearances.originalFile: grail:14599 (VJC) 2024 H2 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Combines $pV = NkT$ with $\frac{1}{2}m\langle c^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2}kT$ and a square-root scaling.
questions.misconception: The r.m.s. speed is proportional to temperature

explanation.body:
From $pV = NkT$: the volume stays the same and the pressure doubles, so the temperature also doubles.

Initial: $\frac{1}{2}m\langle c^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2}kT$. Final: $\frac{1}{2}m\langle c_f^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k(2T)$.

So $\sqrt{\langle c_f^2 \rangle} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{\langle c^2 \rangle} = 1.4c$.

perOption.A: Halves the speed; the temperature increases, so the r.m.s. speed must increase.
perOption.B: Uses $1/\sqrt{2}$, wrongly assuming the temperature halves.
perOption.C: Correct. $T$ doubles, so $c_{\text{rms}}$ increases by $\sqrt{2}$.
perOption.D: Forgets the square root: $\langle c^2 \rangle$ doubles, not $c_{\text{rms}}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two monoatomic ideal gases X and Y are mixed together in a sealed container. The molar mass of Y is twice that of X. At thermodynamic temperature $T$, the kinetic energy and root-mean-square speed of an atom of X are given by $E$ and $V$ respectively.

What is the kinetic energy and root-mean-square speed of an atom of Y at temperature $T$?

| | kinetic energy | root-mean-square speed |
|---|---|---|
| A | $E$ | $0.71V$ |
| B | $E$ | $V$ |
| C | $E$ | $1.4V$ |
| D | $2E$ | $0.71V$ |

stemImage.alt: Question 17: Two monoatomic ideal gases X and Y are mixed together in a sealed container. The molar mass of Y is twice that of X. At thermodynamic temperature T, the kinetic

appearances.originalFile: grail:19928 VJC 2025 J2 H2 Phy Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Applying ⟨KE⟩ = 3/2 kT and v_rms ∝ 1/√m to two gases.
questions.misconception: Thinking heavier gas atoms have more kinetic energy at the same temperature

explanation.body:
The mean kinetic energy of an atom of a monoatomic ideal gas is $E = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$, independent of mass. Both gases are at $T$, so the KE of an atom of Y is also $E$.

For X: $\tfrac{3}{2}kT = \tfrac{1}{2}mV^2$. For Y: $\tfrac{3}{2}kT = \tfrac{1}{2}(2m)V_Y^2$.

Comparing, $V^2 = 2V_Y^2$, so $V_Y = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}}\,V = 0.71V$.

perOption.A: Correct. Same KE at the same $T$; $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$.
perOption.B: Assumes rms speed is independent of mass; equal KE with double mass means lower speed.
perOption.C: Inverts the mass dependence; the heavier atom moves more slowly.
perOption.D: Mean KE depends only on temperature, not on mass, so it is not doubled.

questions.stem: An ideal gas is held in a container of volume V at pressure P. The root-mean-square (r.m.s) speed of a gas molecule under these conditions is u. If the volume and pressure are now changed to 2V and 2P respectively, what will be the r.m.s speed of a molecule?
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is held in a container of volume V at pressure P. The root-mean-square (r.m.s) speed of a gas molecule under these conditions is u. If the volume and pressure are now changed to 2V and 2P respectively, what will be the r.m.s speed of a molecule? A u B 2u C 2u D 4u

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combine the ideal-gas law with the kinetic-energy relation before taking the speed ratio.
questions.misconception: Treating r.m.s. speed as proportional to the pressure–volume product.

explanation.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, and the ideal-gas law gives $PV=NkT$. Combining them gives $c_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3PV/(Nm)}$, so for a fixed amount of gas $c_{\mathrm{rms}}\propto\sqrt{PV}$. Therefore $u'/u=\sqrt{(2P)(2V)/(PV)}=2$, giving $u'=2u$.

perOption.A: Treats $PV$ as unchanged when both factors double.
perOption.B: Accounts for doubling only one of pressure and volume.
perOption.C: Correct. The pressure–volume product quadruples.
perOption.D: Scales the r.m.s. speed directly with $PV$.

Two thermally insulated cylinders A and B are connected by a tube of negligible volume, as shown.

[Diagram: cylinder A, $2.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, $3.4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, 300 K, connected via a tube with tap T to cylinder B, $1.6\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, $4.9\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$.]

Initially, tap T is closed and the cylinders contain an ideal gas at different pressures. Cylinder A contains 0.34 mol of gas and cylinder B contains 0.20 mol of gas. When tap T is opened, the pressure of the gas in both cylinders is $3.9\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

What is the final temperature of the gas?

A 320 K  B 360 K  C 380 K  D 390 K

questions.difficultyReason: Single application of the ideal gas equation to the combined gas, with unit conversion.

explanation.body:
Apply $pV = nRT$ to the total amount of gas after the tap is opened:

$(3.9\times10^{5})(2.5 + 1.6)\times10^{3}\times10^{-6} = (0.34 + 0.20)(8.31)\,T$

$T = 360\ \mathrm{K}$

questions.stemText: The r.m.s. speed of the atoms of an ideal gas at 330 K is increased by 20%. What is the new temperature of the gas? A 230 K B 275 K C 396 K D 475 K

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Single proportionality, but the square is a common trap.
questions.misconception: Taking temperature proportional to r.m.s. speed

explanation.body:
$U = \frac{3}{2}NkT = \frac{1}{2}Nm\langle c^2\rangle$, so $\frac{T}{c_{rms}^2}$ is constant.

$\frac{330}{c_{rms}^2} = \frac{T_{final}}{(1.20\,c_{rms})^2}$, giving $T_{final} = 330 \times 1.44 = 475\ \mathrm{K}$.

perOption.A: Divides by $1.2^2$ instead of multiplying.
perOption.B: Divides by 1.2 instead of multiplying by $1.2^2$.
perOption.C: Assumes $T \propto c_{rms}$ rather than $T \propto c_{rms}^2$.
perOption.D: Correct. $T \propto c_{rms}^2$: $330 \times 1.44$.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising the common pressure and relating gas mass to volume and temperature.
questions.misconception: Assuming the volumes alone determine the mass ratio.

explanation.body: The narrow tube has negligible volume, and the containers have the same pressure at steady state. With gas mass $m'$ and molar mass $M$, $pV=nRT=(m'/M)RT$. Equating the pressures gives $\frac{m(300)}{2V}=\frac{m'_Y(400)}{V}$, so $m'_Y=\frac38m$.

perOption.A: This mass would make the pressure in Y lower than in X.
